title: Capstone: Enterprise Cloud Threat-Hunting Dashboard
summary: Leadership wants one place to see security across a multi-cloud estate. In this capstone you stand up a Microsoft Sentinel workspace, ingest signals from Entra ID, Microsoft 365, Azure Activity, and AWS, and write a custom KQL analytics rule that detects impossible travel, the same user signing in from two distant locations within minutes. You then connect that detection to a Logic App playbook that disables the account and routes it to PIM and analyst review, and you build a Workbook dashboard for leadership. You will write the KQL, build the SOAR automation, validate the end-to-end flow, and package it as a portfolio-grade SIEM/SOAR project. It draws directly on Modules 4 and 5.
objectives: Stand up a Microsoft Sentinel workspace and connect Entra, M365, Azure Activity, and AWS data connectors
Write a custom KQL scheduled analytics rule that detects impossible-travel / concurrent anomalous logins
Map alert entities (account, IP) so detections drive automated response
Build a Logic App playbook that disables the account and routes the case to PIM and analyst review
Validate the detection-to-response flow end to end with controlled test sign-ins
Build a Workbook dashboard and assemble the KQL, playbook, and screenshots into a hireable portfolio artifact

quiz.q: Why is Microsoft Sentinel a strong choice for centralized multi-cloud security reporting in this scenario?
options: It only works with Azure resources and nothing else
It is a cloud-native SIEM/SOAR that ingests signals from Microsoft and non-Microsoft sources (including AWS) and combines detection, hunting, and automated response in one workspace
It replaces the need for any data connectors
It stores data only on local analyst machines
quiz.why: Sentinel is a cloud-native SIEM and SOAR. With data connectors it ingests Entra, M365, Azure Activity, and AWS (CloudTrail/security data), then lets you run KQL analytics, hunting, workbooks, and playbooks over the unified data, which is exactly what 'one place to see security across multi-cloud' requires.

quiz.q: In the impossible-travel KQL, why do you join the sign-in table to itself on the same UserPrincipalName?
options: To remove duplicate rows from the table
To compare two sign-in events for the same user and measure the time and distance between two different locations
Because KQL requires every query to use join
To convert the table into a workbook
quiz.why: A self-join pairs each sign-in with another sign-in by the same user, so you can compute the time gap and the geographic distance between the two events. That pairing is what lets you flag the same identity appearing in two far-apart places within an implausibly short window.

quiz.q: What is the role of entity mapping in the analytics rule?
options: It makes the query run faster
It tags fields like the account and IP as recognized entities so the incident is investigable and so playbooks can act on those entities automatically
It encrypts the alert
It is only needed for workbooks, not rules
quiz.why: Entity mapping identifies the account, host, and IP within each alert. This enriches the incident graph for investigation and, critically, gives the playbook the structured entity (the account) it needs to disable the right user automatically rather than parsing free text.

quiz.q: Why route the response through a Logic App playbook that disables the account AND sends it to PIM/analyst review, rather than only disabling the account silently?
options: Because Logic Apps cannot disable accounts
To combine fast automated containment with human oversight and a path to restore least-privilege access, reducing both risk and the chance of a disruptive false positive going unreviewed
Because PIM is required to run any Logic App
To make the playbook slower on purpose
quiz.why: Automated disablement contains the threat in seconds, but impossible travel can be a false positive (VPN, corporate proxy). Pairing automation with analyst review and a PIM-governed restore path gives speed without removing human judgment, and ensures access is brought back under least-privilege controls rather than ad hoc.

quiz.q: When validating, how can you safely simulate impossible travel without traveling or using a real attacker?
options: Wait for a real attack to occur in production
Generate test sign-ins for a test account from two different network locations (e.g., a VPN exit in another country) within a short window, or inject crafted sample sign-in logs
Disable all logging during the test
Delete the analytics rule and recreate it
quiz.why: Using a dedicated test account, you can sign in from your normal location and then via a VPN exit node in a distant country within a few minutes, which produces two far-apart sign-ins. Alternatively you can inject crafted sample SigninLogs. Either approach drives the rule without any real compromise.

quiz.q: In two to four sentences, explain the design trade-offs of the impossible-travel rule: what makes it valuable, what causes false positives, and one tuning step you would apply before enabling auto-disable in production.
quiz.answer: Impossible travel is valuable because it catches credential theft and session hijacking that single-event rules miss, the same identity cannot physically be in Massachusetts and abroad ten minutes apart. Its main false-positive sources are corporate VPNs, cloud proxies, mobile carrier NAT, and roaming, which make legitimate users appear to jump locations. Before enabling auto-disable I would tune the rule by excluding known corporate egress IP ranges and trusted named locations, requiring the second sign-in to be from an untrusted or risky IP, and possibly correlating with an Entra ID Protection risk signal, and I might start the playbook in 'require analyst approval' mode rather than fully automatic. This keeps detection sensitive while preventing disruptive mass lockouts.
quiz.why: A strong answer names the detection value (catches what single-event rules miss), concrete false-positive drivers (VPN/proxy/roaming), and at least one real tuning lever (trusted-location/IP exclusion, risk correlation, or analyst-approval gating) before full automation.

Connect Sentinel to Amazon Web Services to ingest AWS service log data

body_markdown:
## Scenario

The CISO is tired of swivel-chairing between the Entra portal, the Microsoft 365 admin center, the Azure portal, and the AWS console to answer one question: 'Are we under attack right now?' Leadership wants **one centralized security dashboard across the multi-cloud estate**, with automated response for the obvious wins. Your capstone delivers exactly that with **Microsoft Sentinel**: a single SIEM/SOAR workspace that ingests identity and cloud signals, detects **impossible travel** (the same user appearing in two distant locations within minutes, classic credential theft), automatically contains the account, and visualizes it all for leadership.

This is the headline project for Modules 4 (Cloud SIEM & SOAR with Sentinel) and 5 (Security Automation with PowerShell, Graph, and Logic Apps). It proves you can run a cloud SOC, write detections in KQL, and automate response, the core of a modern security engineering role.

## Architecture

Five components, left to right:

1. **Ingestion - Data connectors.** A Sentinel workspace on a Log Analytics workspace, with connectors for **Microsoft Entra ID** (SigninLogs, AuditLogs), **Microsoft 365** (Defender/Office activity), **Azure Activity**, and **AWS** (CloudTrail / AWS security data via the S3 connector). Now Entra sign-ins and AWS API activity live in one query surface.
2. **Detection - Custom KQL analytics rule.** A scheduled rule runs the impossible-travel query on **SigninLogs** every few minutes, emitting an alert/incident when the same user signs in from two far-apart locations inside a short window.
3. **Enrichment - Entity mapping.** The rule maps **Account** (UserPrincipalName) and **IP** as entities so the incident is investigable and the playbook can act on the account.
4. **Response - Logic App playbook.** An automation rule triggers a **Sentinel playbook** (Logic App) that **disables the user in Entra ID via Microsoft Graph**, posts the case to the SOC channel/ticket, and routes it to **PIM**/analyst review for a governed restore.
5. **Reporting - Workbook dashboard.** A Sentinel **Workbook** visualizes sign-ins by country, top risky IPs, impossible-travel incidents over time, and AWS activity, the leadership view.

## The impossible-travel KQL

The heart of the project. This scheduled rule self-joins `SigninLogs` to pair two successful sign-ins by the same user, then flags pairs that are geographically far apart but close in time, for example one from Massachusetts and one from a foreign IP within 10 minutes:

```kusto
let timeWindow = 10m;
let lookback = 1h;
let successful =
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
    | where ResultType == 0                 // successful sign-ins only
    | extend City = tostring(LocationDetails.city),
             Country = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion),
             Lat = todouble(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.latitude),
             Lon = todouble(LocationDetails.geoCoordinates.longitude)
    | project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, City, Country, Lat, Lon;
successful
| join kind=inner (
    successful
    | project-rename TimeGenerated2 = TimeGenerated, IPAddress2 = IPAddress,
                     City2 = City, Country2 = Country, Lat2 = Lat, Lon2 = Lon
  ) on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated < TimeGenerated2                     // ordered pair, no self-match
| where TimeGenerated2 - TimeGenerated <= timeWindow        // within the short window
| where Country != Country2 or IPAddress != IPAddress2      // genuinely different origin
| extend DistanceKm = geo_distance_2points(Lon, Lat, Lon2, Lat2) / 1000.0
| where DistanceKm > 500                                    // implausibly far apart
| extend MinutesApart = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated2, TimeGenerated)
| project UserPrincipalName, TimeGenerated, City, Country, IPAddress,
          TimeGenerated2, City2, Country2, IPAddress2, DistanceKm, MinutesApart
```

Key ideas: filter to **successful** sign-ins (`ResultType == 0`), **self-join on UserPrincipalName** to compare two events for one identity, use `geo_distance_2points` for great-circle distance, and require both a large distance and a short time gap. In the rule wizard, set the schedule (run every 5-10 min, lookback 1h), map **Account = UserPrincipalName** and **IP = IPAddress**, and set incident creation on.

## Step-by-step build

**Step 0 - Prerequisites.** An Azure subscription with a Log Analytics workspace, an Entra tenant generating sign-ins, and (optionally) an AWS account for the AWS connector. Use evaluation/free tiers.

**Step 1 - Onboard Sentinel.** Create/choose a Log Analytics workspace and enable Microsoft Sentinel on it.

**Step 2 - Connect data.** Install the **Microsoft Entra ID** connector and enable SigninLogs + AuditLogs (via Diagnostic settings). Add **Microsoft 365** and **Azure Activity** connectors. Add the **Amazon Web Services** connector (S3-based) to pull CloudTrail. Confirm tables populate (`SigninLogs`, `AWSCloudTrail`).

**Step 3 - Create the analytics rule.** New > **Scheduled query rule**; paste the KQL; set frequency/lookback; map entities; enable **Create incidents**; set severity Medium/High.

**Step 4 - Build the playbook.** Create a **Logic App** playbook triggered by *Microsoft Sentinel incident*. Steps: parse the **Account** entity; call **Microsoft Graph** (or the Entra connector) to **disable the user** (`accountEnabled = false`) and/or revoke sessions; post an adaptive card to Teams/create a ticket; add a task to **review in PIM**. Attach it via an **automation rule** so qualifying incidents run it automatically (or with analyst approval).

**Step 5 - Build the workbook.** Create a **Workbook** with tiles: sign-ins by country (map), impossible-travel incidents over time, top source IPs, and AWS CloudTrail activity. This is the leadership dashboard.

## Validation / Testing

Drive the whole chain safely:

- **Simulate impossible travel:** with a dedicated **test account**, sign in from your normal location, then within a few minutes sign in again through a **VPN exit node in another country**. Two far-apart successful sign-ins now exist in `SigninLogs`. (Alternatively, inject crafted sample `SigninLogs` rows.)
- **Confirm detection:** run the KQL manually in Logs to see the pair returned; then wait for the scheduled rule to fire and create an **incident** with the account and IP entities mapped.
- **Confirm response:** verify the playbook ran, the **test account is disabled** in Entra (and sessions revoked), the **Teams card/ticket** posted, and a **PIM/analyst review** task exists.
- **Confirm false-positive handling:** repeat using a *trusted* corporate VPN IP that you have added to **trusted named locations**, and show the rule does NOT fire, demonstrating your tuning.
- **Confirm dashboard:** the Workbook shows the incident on the map and timeline.

Keep a *Stage | Test | Expected | Observed | Pass/Fail* table and capture screenshots at each stage.

## What to put in your portfolio

- **Architecture diagram**: connectors -> Sentinel -> analytics rule -> playbook -> workbook.
- **The KQL detection** as a clean, commented `.kql` file in your repo (this is the single most impressive artifact, interviewers will ask you to read it line by line).
- **The playbook**: exported Logic App JSON / ARM template, with the account-disable and PIM-routing steps.
- **Workbook export** (JSON) and screenshots of the leadership dashboard.
- **A short demo video** of the impossible-travel simulation triggering the incident, the auto-disable, and the dashboard updating.
- **A design doc** covering the detection logic, the false-positive tuning, and why you gated full automation behind analyst review.

Resume bullet, impact-first: 'Built a Microsoft Sentinel SIEM/SOAR with multi-cloud connectors (Entra, M365, Azure, AWS); authored a KQL impossible-travel detection wired to a Logic App playbook that auto-disables compromised accounts and routes them to PIM review, containing credential-theft incidents in under a minute.'

A scheduled KQL rule runs every few minutes to detect impossible travel. Entity mapping turns the matched account and IP into structured entities. Then a Logic App playbook responds automatically, and a Workbook dashboard reports the picture to leadership.

slides.title: The Impossible-Travel KQL
bullets: Filter to successful sign-ins (ResultType == 0)
Self-join SigninLogs on UserPrincipalName to pair two events
geo_distance_2points gives great-circle distance
Flag pairs that are far apart but minutes apart in time
slides.code:
successful
| join kind=inner (successful | project-rename TimeGenerated2=TimeGenerated, Lat2=Lat, Lon2=Lon, Country2=Country) on UserPrincipalName
| where TimeGenerated < TimeGenerated2
| where TimeGenerated2 - TimeGenerated <= 10m
| extend DistanceKm = geo_distance_2points(Lon, Lat, Lon2, Lat2)/1000.0
| where DistanceKm > 500
slides.narration: This is the heart of the project. We take successful sign-ins only, then self-join the table to itself on the user principal name so each row pairs two sign-ins for the same identity. We compute the great-circle distance with geo_distance_2points and keep only pairs that are more than five hundred kilometers apart yet within a ten-minute window. The same person cannot be in Massachusetts and abroad ten minutes apart, that is your detection.

slides.title: From Detection to Response
bullets: Map Account = UserPrincipalName and IP = IPAddress as entities
Automation rule triggers a Logic App playbook on the incident
Playbook calls Graph to disable the account and revoke sessions
It also routes the case to PIM and analyst review
slides.narration: Entity mapping is what makes response possible: by tagging the account and IP as entities, the playbook receives a structured account to act on instead of parsing text. An automation rule fires the Logic App, which calls Microsoft Graph to disable the user and revoke sessions, posts a card to the SOC, and creates a PIM review task. That pairing of fast automation with human oversight is deliberate.

slides.title: Tuning: Avoid Disruptive False Positives
bullets: VPNs, proxies, carrier NAT, and roaming cause false positives
Exclude corporate egress IPs and trusted named locations
Require the second sign-in to be from an untrusted/risky IP
Consider analyst-approval mode before full auto-disable
slides.narration: Impossible travel is powerful but noisy. Corporate VPNs and cloud proxies make legitimate users appear to teleport. Before you let it auto-disable accounts, exclude known corporate egress ranges and trusted named locations, require the distant sign-in to come from an untrusted or risky IP, and consider correlating with an Entra ID Protection risk signal. Many teams start the playbook in require-approval mode to avoid mass lockouts while they build confidence.

slides.title: Validation: Drive the Whole Chain Safely
bullets: Use a test account: sign in locally, then via a foreign VPN within minutes
Run the KQL in Logs, then confirm the scheduled rule creates an incident
Verify the account is disabled and a PIM review task exists
Show a trusted-VPN sign-in does NOT fire (your tuning works)
slides.narration: To test safely, use a dedicated test account: sign in from your normal location, then through a VPN exit in another country within a few minutes. Run the KQL manually to see the pair, then let the scheduled rule create an incident, and confirm the playbook disabled the account and opened a PIM review. Crucially, repeat from a trusted VPN you have allow-listed and show the rule stays quiet, that proves your tuning. Keep a pass/fail table and screenshots.

Lead the resume bullet with impact: containing credential-theft incidents in under a minute across multi-cloud.
